title: Accelerator ABI and Driver Graceful Degradation ADR
author: Michael Chen
body:
Summary

This ADR defines the Accelerator ABI (application binary interface) and the runtime-side driver graceful-degradation policy for heterogeneous accelerator fleets (GPU, TPU-like ASICs, and vendor-provided inference accelerators). The goal is a small, well-specified handshake and capability set that: 1) allows the runtime to negotiate performance/precision tradeoffs with device drivers; 2) exposes a deterministic degradation path when an accelerator cannot satisfy requested guarantees; and 3) provides operational signals for capacity, thermal, and error states so higher layers (routing, fallback) can make policy decisions.

Context and motivation

Redwood's serving runtime runs across mixed hardware: cloud GPUs with different memory/compute, vendor inference chips with quantization-aware runtimes, and experimental on-prem ASICs for Private deployments. Historically each driver exposed a different surface (promises about sequence-length limits, supported quantization, KV cache semantics), which led to fragile fallbacks and silent quality regressions. Operations has observed incidents where a node reported "healthy" but silently served half-precision tensors, creating subtle hallucination regressions in downstream evals. We need a minimal ABI and a deterministic downgrade model so the orchestration and routing layers can react before customer-visible quality drops.

Decision (what we are adopting)

We adopt a two-part contract:

1) Accelerator ABI (driver runtime surface)
- A JSON capability manifest returned during driver handshake with these required fields: vendor, model, memory_bytes, peak_fp32_throughput, supported_precisions (list), max_sequence_length, kv_cache_model (none|keyseg|segmented), supported_quant_modes (list), fail_modes (list of canonical failure codes).
- A gRPC control channel for health + telemetry that emits structured events: THERMAL_WARNING, MEMORY_PRESSURE, DRIVER_DEGRADATION(start/end), ARTIFACT_ERRORS. Events include numeric fields (temp_celsius, available_bytes, eviction_count).
- Deterministic downgrade functions exposed by drivers: get_degradation_path(requested_precision) -> ordered list of fallback precisions and a max-acceptable-seq-length for each step.

2) Graceful-degradation policy (runtime orchestration expectations)
- If a driver indicates DRIVER_DEGRADATION or memory pressure that will affect >P% of requests in next T seconds, the runtime must:
  a) Mark node as "degrading" and emit a metric (accelerator.node.degradation{reason}).
  b) For new requests, consult degradation path and either re-route to compatible node, fall back to a quantized variant, or invoke a lower-fidelity model per client policy.
  c) For in-flight requests, attempt best-effort KV-preserving re-execution (see runbook) but avoid silent precision demotion unless explicitly allowed by the tenant's model policy.

Rationale

- Small manifest + events provide actionable signals without locking in per-vendor RPCs.
- Centralizing downgrade logic in drivers avoids guessing behavior and ensures the runtime can reason about end-to-end effects (e.g., seq length vs precision tradeoff).
- Separating "allowed by tenant policy" from automatic demotion prevents silent regressions for customers with strict fidelity requirements.

Alternatives considered

1) Do nothing / keep vendor-specific surfaces
   - Pros: no immediate engineering cost
   - Cons: repeated incidents, unpredictable fallbacks, poor observability for quality regressions (rejected).

2) Full feature-rich driver RPC (rich schema for every kernel)
   - Pros: maximum expressivity
   - Cons: long vendor integration time, brittle across versions (rejected).

3) Runtime-only heuristic demotion (runtime interprets raw metrics and decides)
   - Pros: driver-agnostic
   - Cons: wrong assumptions across devices; drivers have the ground truth (rejected).

Implementation specification

1) Manifest schema (JSON example)
{
  "vendor": "string",
  "device_model": "string",
  "memory_bytes": 68719476736,
  "peak_fp32_throughput": 12000.0,
  "supported_precisions": ["fp32","fp16","int8*"],
  "max_sequence_length": 4096,
  "kv_cache_model": "segmented",
  "supported_quant_modes": ["static8","dynamic8","awq"],
  "fail_modes": ["OOM","THERMAL","DRIVER_FAULT"]
}

2) Control channel: gRPC proto (summary)
- Service: AcceleratorControl
- RPCs: GetManifest(), StreamEvents(stream Event) -> ack, SetThrottle(level) -> ack
- Event structure: {timestamp_ms, node_id, code, numeric_map, text}

3) Degradation API (driver-side function)
- get_degradation_path(requested_precision: string, requested_sequence: int) -> list of {precision, max_sequence_length, estimated_throughput_ratio}

Operational runbook (short)

Triggers and immediate actions:
1) Event THERMAL_WARNING with temp_celsius > 85 for 30s -> put node into read-only drain and notify SRE.
2) DRIVER_DEGRADATION with predicted_available_bytes < requested_memory -> mark degrading, reduce offerable concurrency by 50% and trigger rescheduling.

Manual recovery steps:
1) For transient thermal events: verify cooling system, evict long-running ephemeral jobs, restart driver process if required.
2) For persistent artifact errors: collect driver logs / dmesg, escalate to vendor with manifest and event stream.

Routing & API implications

- API layer must include these fields in the request envelope: preferred_fidelity (strict|best-effort|cost-optimized) and allow_demote boolean.
- Default tenant policy: preferred_fidelity=best-effort, allow_demote=false. Allowing demote requires explicit opt-in by the customer and is surfaced in Console settings.

Testing and acceptance criteria

- Unit: manifest parsing, event handling, degradation-path evaluation.
- Integration: simulate driver events (thermal, OOM) in testbed and assert runtime re-routes or rejects per tenant policy.
- Quality regression: run prompt-suite CI (refer to prompt-suite-ci-contract-testing-guidelines) before and after simulated demotion; metrics: BLEU/ROUGE analogs and hallucination rate must not regress beyond tenant thresholds.

Metrics to monitor

- accelerator.node.degradation.count by code
- accelerator.request.demoted.count by tenant and model
- end_to_end_quality_regressions.per_model (linked to evals)
- routing_fallbacks.per_minute

Rollout plan

1) Stage 0: Spec review and vendor alignment (2 weeks).
2) Stage 1: Driver shim implementation for two vendor drivers and testbed integration (6 weeks).
3) Stage 2: Runtime support (handshake, event processing, routing changes) in canary (4 weeks).
4) Stage 3: Tenant opt-in on Dedicated and Private (2 weeks).
5) Stage 4: Full launch for Hosted (after 8 weeks of canary stability).

Owners and contacts

Open questions and future work

- How to represent approximate numeric fidelity (e.g., AWQ variants with mixed blocks)? We propose a small extension to the manifest to include per-layer fidelity profiles in a later ADR.
- Should the runtime be allowed to force demotion for system safety (e.g., to avoid cascading OOMs)? Current decision: only when "system_safety" flag present in tenant policy (requires legal/product sign-off).

Appendix A: Example degradation path table

| requested_precision | step | fallback_precision | max_seq | throughput_ratio | notes |
|---------------------|------|--------------------|---------|------------------|-------|
| fp32                | 0    | fp32               | 4096    | 1.0              | native |
| fp32                | 1    | fp16               | 4096    | 0.65             | reduced numerical headroom |
| fp32                | 2    | int8               | 2048    | 0.35             | quantized; requires calibration |

Appendix B: Example tenant request headers (JSON)
{
  "tenant_id": "t-12345",
  "model": "redwood-base-13b",
  "preferred_fidelity": "best-effort",
  "allow_demote": false
}
